/uk-news/2026/sep/27/arrests-suspected-t.headline: Five arrested for alleged terrorism offences after ‘major incident’ near RAF Fairford
/uk-news/2026/sep/27/arrests-suspected-t.excerpt: Counter-terrorism police are leading the investigation in which five men were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences near an RAF base used in US attacks against Iran. After the declaration of a major incident at RAF Fairford, a bomb squad was sent to the village of Whelford and extra security measures were put in place, including the fortification of entrances to the base. Roadblocks and armed police have been seen in the area over the weekend. After their initial arrest over explosives offences, the five men detained early on Sunday morning were further arrested later in the day on suspicion of the preparation of a terrorist act, the Metropolitan police said. Eighty-five households were evacuated and taken to a leisure centre in the early hours of Sunday morning, while the army’s bomb squad examined three suspicious vehicles. Police said they were working to get local people back into their homes as soon as possible. Materials were seized after the arrests by armed officers under the Explosives Act and were being examined to see how dangerous they were and whether they were technically capable of being used in an attack, the Guardian understands. The operation was not intelligence-led, suggesting that investigators had not known about any potential plot in advance.
/uk-news/2026/sep/27/arrests-suspected-t.trail: Men held also suspected of explosives offences as homes evacuated near British airbase used in US attacks on Iran

/uk-news/2026/sep/27/arrests-suspected-t.headline: NHS trust removes 10 staff from duty over Noah Woods data breach
/uk-news/2026/sep/27/arrests-suspected-t.excerpt: An NHS trust has apologised after the medical records of three-year-old Noah Woods were accessed by unauthorised people after his disappearance. Noah was found dead in a pond in Brantham, Suffolk, after going missing from a playground. More than 1,300 members of the public joined a search for the boy before police discovered his body. A spokesperson for East Suffolk and North Essex NHS foundation trust said 10 employees had been “removed from active duty or suspended whilst investigations are concluded”. The trust said in a statement that disciplinary action was being explored as a result. Dr Martin Mansfield, deputy chief medical officer at the trust, said: “We have apologised unreservedly to Noah Woods’ family for the extra anguish this breach of trust has caused them at an already devastating time.” He added that unauthorised access of patient data was “completely unacceptable” and said the matter had been reported to the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO). Mansfield added: “As soon as we became aware of concerns that Noah’s medical records may have been viewed inappropriately, we launched an urgent internal investigation. Immediate steps were also taken to secure the records and prevent further access that was not for a legitimate, clinical reason.” The chief executive of NHS England, Sir Jim Mackey, said on Friday that NHS staff would be suspended immediately if found snooping on patients’ records for unauthorised reasons.
/uk-news/2026/sep/27/arrests-suspected-t.trail: East Suffolk and North Essex NHS trust apologises after illicit access of medical records of toddler who died in Brantham

/uk-news/2026/sep/27/arrests-suspected-t.headline: ‘People are standing up and fighting back’: the north Devon revolt against a vast AI datacentre
/uk-news/2026/sep/27/arrests-suspected-t.excerpt: The datacentre revolt spreading across the US has reached the rolling hills of north Devon in an uprising against a planned hyperscale AI data campus in the middle of a globally protected landscape. Perched on an inland cliff, the town of Great Torrington has views that stretch for miles over the landscape of the Unesco biosphere reserve in which it sits, taking in the winding River Torridge and rolling acres of wooded valley and wildflower meadows. Pastoral and peaceful, its history was notably punctured by violence in 1646 when the royalists’ resistance in the first English civil war was brought to an end by the parliamentarian New Model Army in a battle fought out in the narrow streets in heavy rain and darkness. Today, a very 21st-century threat is rippling through the same country lanes as the AI boom reaches the pubs, churches and parish halls of Great Torrington and its surrounding villages. The countryside that makes up the biosphere has been selected by a British company, Xlinks, to house a 1.5GW AI datacentre, one of the largest in Europe, as well as a vast 1.8GW battery energy storage system, or BESS. About 344 hectares (850 acres) of countryside have been secured for the huge campus, with five vast buildings ranging in height from 50 to 130 feet. Listed buildings on the site, Xlinks says, will be relocated and transformed into a visitor centre.
/uk-news/2026/sep/27/arrests-suspected-t.trail: Plans for one of Europe’s largest AI campuses in a Unesco-designated reserve have sparked a fierce local backlash

/uk-news/2026/sep/27/arrests-suspected-t.headline: Andy Burnham announces new homes scheme for first-time buyers
/uk-news/2026/sep/27/arrests-suspected-t.excerpt: A new help-to-buy scheme aimed at giving first-time buyers who cannot rely on the “bank of mum and dad” is to be introduced in a big policy announcement by Andy Burnham. The programme, called “Your first home”, is intended to help buyers in England who have a regular income but have been unable to save for a large deposit or don’t have financial support from their family. Under the scheme, first-time buyers will get a 20% equity loan to help them buy a new-build home, with an initial interest free period and a requirement of a minimum deposit of just 2.5%. Household income caps and a deposit cap will be introduced to exclude those on the biggest salaries and with big savings pots, with the scheme targeted at those who may struggle to buy a home on their own. Price caps will ensure people can only buy modest houses. In an interview with the Guardian on the eve of Labour’s party conference in Liverpool, the prime minister said: “Too many young people are struggling with housing, with many giving up hope on ever having a home to call their own. “So we are going to help more first-time buyers on to the housing ladder, especially those who can’t call on the bank of mum and dad.
/uk-news/2026/sep/27/arrests-suspected-t.trail: Exclusive: Policy initiative for England will help more young people on to property ladder, prime minister tells Guardian

/politics/2026/sep/27/andy-burnham-elect.headline: Angela Rayner stands by attack on care worker visa reforms ahead of Labour conference
/politics/2026/sep/27/andy-burnham-elect.excerpt: Angela Rayner has stood by her criticism of Home Office reforms that would make it harder for foreign care workers to claim permanent residence in the UK, describing them as “disruptive”. Last year, Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, announced that low paid migrants on jobs below graduate level would have to be in the country for 15 years before applying for settlement. Rayner previously attacked the plans as being “un-British”. The policy was devised under the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer, to ease voter concerns about net migration numbers. Andy Burnham, who succeeded Starmer in July, is understood to be uneasy about aspects of the proposals and is considering exempting workers who have already moved to the UK. More than 100 Labour MPs are opposed to the reforms, as are many trade unions. Hinting at a potential schism in the cabinet in the run-up to Burnham’s first Labour conference as leader, Rayner said the changes would unfairly penalise staff who had “moved their lives here to look after our loved ones”. The housing secretary, herself a former care worker who left school at 16, had been critical of the plans before she rejoined the cabinet. She was forced to resign as deputy prime minister last year amid a row over unpaid stamp duty on a flat she had bought in Hove.
/politics/2026/sep/27/andy-burnham-elect.trail: Housing secretary says Home Office moved goalposts with ‘disruptive’ change to permanent residence rules

/politics/2026/sep/27/andy-burnham-elect.headline: Labour must reunite progressive voters to win the next election, says Lucy Powell
/politics/2026/sep/27/andy-burnham-elect.excerpt: Labour must “reunite the progressive voter coalition” if it is to take advantage of a split on the right and win the next election, the party’s deputy leader has said. Lucy Powell, who won the race to be deputy leader 12 months ago with a warning that Labour was losing the fight to be heard as Reform UK surged, said the government now had a second chance under Andy Burnham. In an interview with the Guardian, Powell said the party had clearly required a “change of leader” to revive its fortunes and tell a better story, after becoming “too technical and pessimistic”. Labour’s improved poll ratings have led to speculation this week that Andy Burnham will call a snap election, but the prime minister rejected that on Friday and said the next contest would be in 2029. However, the Labour conference will get underway this weekend with polls beginning to show for the first time in almost two years that Labour might be within touching distance of winning a majority at the next election – 12 months on from polls that suggested Reform UK could win a huge victory. Powell said Labour was beginning to get a hearing again and should not be embarrassed to show its values clearly. “If you look at the evidence from recent elections – right across the board – it’s clear that whichever party manages to unite its voter coalition is the one that wins. And for us on the left, that means bringing our centre-left bloc back together,” she said.
/politics/2026/sep/27/andy-burnham-elect.trail: The deputy leader wants the party to take advantage of a split on the right and not be embarrassed to show its values

/politics/2026/sep/28/ed-miliband-labour.headline: Tony Blair says Britain should work towards rejoining EU in next 10 years
/politics/2026/sep/28/ed-miliband-labour.excerpt: Britain should work towards rejoining the EU in the next decade, Tony Blair has said, adding to growing pressure on Andy Burnham to abandon Labour’s reluctance to revisit the 2016 referendum. The former prime minister has urged Burnham to use his 10-year plan in November to put the country’s membership of the union back on the table, a decade after it voted to leave. In a paper entitled A Path to Rejoining a Reformed Europe, the Tony Blair Institute (TBI) calls for the UK to accept free movement of people and make a financial contribution as the price of entry. The intervention comes after Burnham declined to rule out promising to rejoin the EU in the next Labour manifesto, though it also threatens to reopen the deep rifts caused by the vote 10 years ago. In a foreword to the paper, Blair argues: “Britain should signal an intention if the terms are right to enter into a structured formal relationship with Europe and initiate a process of negotiation where everything is on the table but nothing agreed until everything is agreed.” TBI researchers say in the paper itself: “Over the next decade, Britain should work towards the ambition of rejoining a significantly reformed EU.” Blair is the latest in a series of Labour figures to back rejoining the EU.
/politics/2026/sep/28/ed-miliband-labour.trail: Andy Burnham under pressure to revisit Brexit as poll suggests pledge to rejoin could boost Labour’s electoral chances

/politics/2026/sep/28/ed-miliband-labour.headline: Andy Burnham does not rule out Brexit reversal being in next Labour manifesto
/politics/2026/sep/28/ed-miliband-labour.excerpt: Andy Burnham has opened the door to fighting the next election on the UK rejoining the EU, but said his immediate priority was continuing to rebuild bridges with European allies. The prime minister, who will hold his first meeting with the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, on Tuesday, did not rule out including reversing Brexit in Labour’s next manifesto – but suggested the country should focus on securing closer trading ties first. Ministers have expressed fears privately that the EU reset has lost significant momentum since Burnham became prime minister, and a summit on the issue is likely to be delayed again unless the bloc agrees to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry. Burnham has said he will stick to Keir Starmer’s red lines this side of an election, but he is under pressure from Labour MPs who opposed Brexit to change tack, in part because of the potential boost to growth, even though his own seat of Makerfield voted to leave. Asked by reporters on his flight to New York on Monday for the UN general assembly whether he could rule out a reversal of Brexit being in the next Labour manifesto, he said: “Our focus at the moment is on a UK/EU summit which we hope will take place later this year. “My immediate priority is to build on the good work that Keir did in rebuilding bridges. Because those bridges were broken in the early part of this decade. And Keir did a good job in re-establishing that relationship.
/politics/2026/sep/28/ed-miliband-labour.trail: PM says immediate focus is on rebuilding bridges with EU as he prepares for first meeting with Ursula von der Leyen

/politics/2026/sep/28/ed-miliband-labour.headline: ‘Sweat the asset’: new development minister plots path to make UK aid count
/politics/2026/sep/28/ed-miliband-labour.excerpt: The development minister, Kirsty McNeill, has declared herself “a huge believer in aid”, as she reaffirmed Labour’s manifesto pledge to return to a target of 0.7% of national income spending. McNeill, a former adviser to Gordon Brown and senior executive at Save the Children, declined to give any timetable, repeating the formula that the government would work towards the target “when fiscal circumstances allow”. But she made a full-throated argument for the benefits of aid – as well as promising to build new “agile partnerships” to work on development challenges. “I’m a huge believer in aid; I’m a huge believer in the quality of British aid, and when you have more of it, you can have more impact. And I think it’s important that colleagues hear that underscored,” she said. Repeating the manifesto pledge that Labour made before the 2024 general election to return to 0.7% – instead slashing aid the next year – McNeill insisted that in the Burnham government, “everyone from the prime minister down is a believer in the spirit that animated that manifesto”. McNeill will be setting out her priorities in a speech to charities and campaigners at the New Economics Foundation thinktank on Monday. She will announce that the government is making up to £15m available via its humanitarian crisis fund to support preventive action in countries most at risk from El Niño. “It will just do very practical things like vaccinate livestock and get cash to farmers to provide supplies,” she said.
/politics/2026/sep/28/ed-miliband-labour.trail: Kirsty McNeill reaffirms Labour’s 0.7% of GDP pledge and promises value for money to allay voter concerns

/politics/2026/sep/28/ed-miliband-labour.headline: Burnham to visit Ukraine with promise of boost for Kyiv’s long-range missiles
/politics/2026/sep/28/ed-miliband-labour.excerpt: Britain will boost Ukraine’s capacity to make its own long-range missiles, Andy Burnham will announce on Monday, as he travels to Kyiv for the country’s independence day on his first foreign visit as prime minister. Burnham will arrive in the Ukrainian capital on Monday morning at a crucial time in the war, with Kyiv braced for another wave of Russian missile attacks and the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, facing his most direct domestic challenge. The UK prime minister will use the trip to announce that the UK government will allow the European defence company MBDA to declassify information about UK-made components of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow/Scalp missiles to help Ukraine build its own version. While the announcement will probably take years to have an impact on the war, it is likely to escalate tensions with Moscow at an already fraught moment in UK-Russian relations. Burnham said in a statement on Sunday night: “On Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes. “I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine’s security is our security. “The friendship between our two countries will long outlast Russia’s illegal war.
/politics/2026/sep/28/ed-miliband-labour.trail: PM will use independence day trip to announce sharing of classified information about Storm Shadow components

/politics/2026/sep/28/ed-miliband-labour.headline: Cabinet ministers’ mobile numbers found online after Burnham targeted
/politics/2026/sep/28/ed-miliband-labour.excerpt: At least three UK cabinet ministers have had their personal mobile phone numbers published online, amid mounting concern over the security of senior politicians after Andy Burnham was targeted by an impersonation scam. The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, the justice secretary, Alex Norris, and the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, had their numbers available online with their names. A reference containing Streeting’s number has since been removed, a source told the Guardian, noting he does all his government business on his official government phone. Officials are understood to be working to take down the others. The leak, first revealed by Politico, come after Burnham exchanged messages with someone posing as Donald Trump’s chief of staff, Susie Wiles. The prime minister was in contact with an unknown individual pretending to be Wiles before concerns were raised about the incident. No messages of significance were sent and the suspicious activity was quickly reported to the appropriate authorities, it is understood. The British embassy in Washington was so concerned it raised the matter with the White House, according to Politico. A UK government spokesperson said: “We do not comment on national security matters.” Downing Street refused to say if any measures had been taken to prevent another breach happening.
/politics/2026/sep/28/ed-miliband-labour.trail: Revelation about security leak follows person pretending to be senior White House aide contacting prime minister

/world/2026/sep/28/trump-xi-jinping-chin.headline: ‘Forcing a reckoning’: How Asia is preparing for a ‘supersized’ El Niño
/world/2026/sep/28/trump-xi-jinping-chin.excerpt: Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region. Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027. The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”. Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño: ‘Climate risk maps’ in China In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees. Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat. In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.
/world/2026/sep/28/trump-xi-jinping-chin.trail: From Sri Lanka to South Korea, governments are preparing for droughts, wildfires, typhoons and floods – with climate plans facing their biggest challenge to date

/world/2026/sep/28/trump-xi-jinping-chin.headline: ‘This is seriously bold’: How China turned Taiwan tensions into a top-rating TV spy drama
/world/2026/sep/28/trump-xi-jinping-chin.excerpt: After shaking off the people trailing her through a crowded market and emerging from a bathroom in disguise, the double agent appears to have escaped. But a sip of water on a plane eventually gets her. She is poisoned after Taiwan’s military intelligence service discovers that she has been working secretly for China. The plot comes from a new Chinese spy drama co-produced by the Ministry of State Security. Since its premiere on 6 September, it has become a TV hit, with a fictionalised take on a subject rarely treated so directly: the modern history of tensions with Taiwan. The series, which will run for 40 episodes, is officially titled The Long Watch in English or Jiaofeng, meaning clashing or “crossing swords” in Chinese. It follows two decades of spies, double agents and intelligence operations between China and Taiwan from the mid-1990s. Jiaofeng mixes fictional characters and locations with real ones such as Taipei, the capital of Taiwan. Yet it remains difficult for analysts to verify how closely the drama follows real events as new episodes continue to be released. While Taiwan’s intelligence services are portrayed as an adversary capable of obtaining sensitive missile information, the drama casts Chinese state security officers as the heroes defending the country against infiltration and theft.
/world/2026/sep/28/trump-xi-jinping-chin.trail: Dismissed in Taiwan as simply propaganda, the Long Watch, or Jiaofeng, has proved a sensation across the strait with its references to real-life crises

/world/2026/sep/28/trump-xi-jinping-chin.headline: ‘TikTok wouldn’t open at all’: Taiwan simulates an internet blackout, with an eye on China threat
/world/2026/sep/28/trump-xi-jinping-chin.excerpt: In Taipei, the streets swiftly empty as air raid sirens ring out and alerts ping on mobile phones. Police officers usher any stragglers into shelters, leaving the capital suddenly deserted. In cities across Taiwan, these kinds of drills are a fact of life every year, amid the growing threat posed by China across the strait, but this time there is something different. Internet speeds were drastically cut on Thursday, simulating a coordinated attack for the first time. Data-heavy services such as video calls, streaming and mobile payments became difficult or impossible to use, while videos on social media barely loaded. However, Wang Chen-wen knows how to reach others. When the sirens sound and her mobile internet begins to grind to a halt, Wang goes to the roof of her 25-storey apartment building, searching for a better radio signal. She connects her phone via Bluetooth to a small, flat device hanging from her bag. Within seconds, she is sending messages without relying on the internet. Minutes later, some of them succeeded in reaching a friend in a neighbouring district. “Testing from Beitou district, Taipei.” “Xinyi district, Taipei.” Messages begin coming in as users share their locations in a group chat being tested on an open-source platform that allows people to use text messages via long-range, low-power radio signals.
/world/2026/sep/28/trump-xi-jinping-chin.trail: Taiwan practised cutting off internet for the first time amid concerns about the safety of the undersea cables that form its ‘digital lifeline’

/world/2026/sep/28/trump-xi-jinping-chin.headline: Taiwan says it was hit by ‘abnormal’ AI-assisted cyber-attack
/world/2026/sep/28/trump-xi-jinping-chin.excerpt: Taiwan says it detected AI-assisted cyber-attacks on government agencies that came from overseas last month, a new kind of threat that has been reported as “first-of-a-kind breach”. The Ministry of Digital Affairs (MDA) said its cybersecurity monitoring units ‌detected the “abnormal attack” targeting government agencies, which began on 20 July. The National Institute of Cyber Security issued a series of warning alerts while it investigated. The Financial Times quoted Dream – an Israeli AI company that detected the intrusion – as saying the attackers used open-source AI agents to build an autonomous hacking tool that behaved like a coordinated cyber team, describing it as a first-of-a-kind breach. Dream was reported as saying that the tool compromised “at least 85 government user accounts, extracting more than 2,500 personnel records before expanding the attack to Taiwan’s nuclear safety agency and at least seven energy companies”. Taiwan has in recent years complained about what it sees as China’s “hybrid warfare” – from daily military drills near the island to disinformation campaigns and cyber-attacks – as Beijing ramps up military and political pressure ⁠on the democratically governed island to force Taipei to accept its claims of sovereignty. Though Taiwanese officials did not direct accusations at China, the FT on Wednesday reported that China-linked hackers were suspected.
/world/2026/sep/28/trump-xi-jinping-chin.trail: Taiwan’s statement comes a day after reports that suspected China-linked hackers had carried out a first-of-a-kind breach

/world/2026/sep/28/trump-xi-jinping-chin.headline: ‘We have lost everything’: extreme rainfall across Asia brings flash floods and typhoons
/world/2026/sep/28/trump-xi-jinping-chin.excerpt: “It rained for 10 days and 10 nights, non-stop – I’d never seen anything like it,” says Anar Gul, a construction worker who lives in the remote district of Dur Baba in eastern Afghanistan. The houses in his village are built from stone and mud, which makes them extremely vulnerable to heavy rains. After days of rain, Gul’s kitchen collapsed and his neighbour, Sayed Afsar Sadat, saw a large part of his house completely destroyed. “Rains like this are coming heavier and earlier each year,” says Sadat. “They are destroying the roads and washing away our crops. It’s impacting us directly.” Last week, torrential rains and flash floods wiped out villages and towns in Afghanistan, leaving at least 31 people dead and hundreds missing. It’s been a similar picture in neighbouring countries, with the monsoon rains sparking chaos across the region. India, Bangladesh and Pakistan have all seen erratic, sudden heavy dumps of water. Jesmin Akter lived in the city of Chattogram, on the south-eastern coast of Bangladesh, which received a record 412.3mm of rainfall in 24 hours in early July, leading to the flash flood that swept through the Banshkhali district where they live. She says her children “understand that we are in a very bad situation”. Overnight the rains took the little they had; their poultry died, their paddy field flooded, their house collapsed and all their belongings in it – children’s books, school bags, toys, clothes, kitchen items – ruined.
/world/2026/sep/28/trump-xi-jinping-chin.trail: From Afghanistan to Taiwan, unprecedented deluge highlights devastating impact of climate breakdown

/world/2026/sep/27/britain-knew-about-ho.headline: ‘I’ll probably feel emotional’: Kindertransport centenarian prepares to revisit site of family separation
/world/2026/sep/27/britain-knew-about-ho.excerpt: Gabriele Keenaghan still remembers the day in April 1939 when she said goodbye to her grandmother at a Vienna railway station for a Kindertransport to Britain – tears were strictly forbidden. “I was apprehensive and I was worried because Nazis in black uniforms were on the platform,” she said. “I was only 12 years old so I think they were frightening … terrifying. “People had been told that there were to be no emotional scenes, they didn’t want any emotion shown by anyone. I tried not to cry. It was very difficult. My grandmother … she smiled.” This week Keenaghan will mark her 100th year by returning to Vienna’s Westbahnhof, a place which changed, if not saved, her life, and there might be tears. “I haven’t thought about how I’ll feel – I probably will feel emotional.” Keenaghan, a retired head teacher, is speaking at her home in North Shields before what will be an epic trip to Vienna with several generations of her family. The plan, hatched for her centenary, was nearly scuppered because Lufthansa cancelled routes from Newcastle. Fortunately, a good samaritan came to the rescue offering the use of a private jet, and the family admit they have been bowled over by the generosity. Keenaghan is 99 but you would never guess. She was awarded the British Empire medal for her services to Holocaust education, recounting what is a remarkable life story in the hope it might bring “kindness, tolerance and acceptance of diversity” in others.
/world/2026/sep/27/britain-knew-about-ho.trail: North Shields’ Gabriele Keenaghan was 12 when she was evacuated from Nazi Austria in 1939. She remembers the shock of leaving her family at Westbahnhof station

/world/2026/sep/27/britain-knew-about-ho.headline: ‘There was absolutely no chance of being a kid’: new exhibition explores how war shapes children’s lives
/world/2026/sep/27/britain-knew-about-ho.excerpt: When John Hajdu was three, his parents gave him a teddy bear small enough to fit into his hands: 86 years later, it is the only surviving object from his childhood. The bear, which the 89-year-old simply calls “teddy”, stayed with him as his father was taken to a labour camp, his mother sent to a concentration camp, and he hid in a non-Jewish neighbour’s cupboard before being forced into the Budapest ghetto. From 31 July, teddy will go on public display for the first time as part of Childhood in War, a new exhibition at the Imperial War Museum, London, examining how conflict shapes children’s lives. Displayed in a recreated second world war bedroom, the bear sits among toys, books and personal possessions that ask visitors to consider what childhood looks like when play, education and family life are disrupted by war. The exhibition combines hundreds of objects with immersive environments, including a full-size railway carriage, a wartime classroom and a cold war living room and kitchen, alongside testimonies from children living through conflicts in places including Ukraine, Sudan and Afghanistan. For Hajdu, teddy represents a childhood interrupted. Before the war, his life was typical of a well-to-do, middle-class Jewish family. By 1944, after years of antisemitic persecution in Hungary, his father had been sent to a labour camp and Hajdu and his mother had been forced into a designated yellow-star house.
/world/2026/sep/27/britain-knew-about-ho.trail: Childhood in War examines what life looks like when play, education and family life is disrupted by hostilities
